clue.text: Guitar players, partly depleted, played round city

indicators.note: something depleted has had part of its stock used up, so a letter goes from the end
to go round something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another
letters that are played with get moved about freely into a new order

parts.note: the word itself, losing its final Y
EC is the postcode district of the City of London

explanation.surface: Some worn-out guitarists strummed their way around a city on tour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guitar players' looks like musicians, but it means the picks they hold. 'Partly' is literal fodder: drop its last letter, rearrange, and wrap it round EC.
explanation.definitionFit: Plectra is the plural of plectrum, the small pick a guitarist uses to pluck or strum the strings.

clue.text: China's one Premier League team

parts.note: rhyming slang: china plate means mate, so a china is a pal
an ace is the one in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: It reads as a boast that China has a team of its own in English football.
explanation.walkthrough: China is Cockney rhyming slang: 'china plate' rhymes with 'mate'. The apostrophe-s stands for 'is', joining the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Crystal Palace is a London football club in the English top flight, commonly called simply Palace by fans and pundits.

clue.text: Named woman in disagreement with Farage?

parts.note: surface reading: a woman with a particular first name
setter's reading: split the name in two and it becomes a view on the European Union that a famous Brexiteer would reject

explanation.surface: A woman who has been named in the press for clashing with a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Nigel Farage campaigned for Britain to leave the European Union. Split the name as EU NICE and it is an opinion he would dispute.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a female given name, so any woman bearing it is a named woman in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Feeding bats to kitten — what about Wed?

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way, so the letters run backwards
food goes inside the one being fed, so one piece is put inside another
bats means crazy, and crazy letters are jumbled into another order

parts.note: taken as written
'eh?' is a way of asking 'what?'

explanation.surface: Someone puzzles over giving bats to a kitten as food, ending with a baffled question about Wednesday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wed' looks like a short form of Wednesday, but it is the verb meaning marry. 'Bats' is not food here; it says the letters are crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: To tie the knot is an informal idiom for getting married, the same action as the verb wed.

clue.text: Forest of Dean a bit different with Queen visiting

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone else's home, so one piece sits within another
something made different has been altered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
R for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: The Forest of Dean looks rather different when the Queen pays a visit.
explanation.walkthrough: The Forest of Dean is a real woodland in Gloucestershire, so the eye reads it as one name; split it into definition, link and fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The Forest of Arden is an ancient woodland in Warwickshire, the setting Shakespeare used for As You Like It.

clue.text: Grumble about predatory type

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
a hunter preys on other creatures

explanation.surface: Someone complains about a predatory character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a link meaning 'concerning', but it supplies C, the circa abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To chunter is a British informal verb for muttering complaints under one's breath, a form of grumbling.

clue.text: As Edward and Don, maybe, changing allegiance

indicators.note: switching allegiance means going from being for something to being against it, so one opposite replaces the other

parts.note: a don is a university teacher, such as a professor

explanation.surface: Two men named Edward and Don both switched sides.
explanation.walkthrough: Pro and con mean for and against, so changing allegiance swaps the PRO of PROFESSOR for CON. A don is a senior academic at Oxford or Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: King Edward the Confessor was an eleventh-century English monarch, so the epithet describes what he was.

clue.text: Not above United? There's more on the other side

parts.note: U is a standard abbreviation for United in team names

parts.words: There's more on the other side
parts.note: PTO, please turn over, is written at the foot of a page continuing overleaf

explanation.surface: A football fan asks whether United are no higher in the table, and is told there is more to read overleaf.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sentence looks like commentary, but it defines PTO, the note at the bottom of a page.
explanation.definitionFit: A limit stated as 'up to ten' means no more than ten, so the phrase means not exceeding or not above.

clue.text: Labour 'Tories' to Vlad annoying

indicators.note: to labour over something is to work it hard, and worked letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
the setter's pseudonym, so the setter himself, me

explanation.surface: The setter finds Labour politicians calling themselves Tories irritating.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour and Tories are rival British parties, so the surface reads as politics; 'Labour' is really a verb telling you to work the letters. A setter's own name means ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tiresome wears out one's patience, making it irritating or annoying in the ordinary sense.

clue.text: Winger from Liverpool sharp

parts.note: Liverpool FC are nicknamed the Reds
tart means sharp in taste

explanation.surface: A sharp wide player has come from Liverpool's football club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winger' suggests a footballer on the flank; in crosswords it often means a bird, something with wings.
explanation.definitionFit: The redstart is a small songbird with a russet tail, and any bird is a creature with wings.

clue.text: Stroll round track — crash initially blocking road

indicators.note: something blocking a passage sits in the middle of it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a lane is a small road

indicators.note: initially points to the start, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A driver going round a racetrack has a crash that blocks the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stroll' looks like a verb for a walk, but it is a surname: Lance Stroll is a Formula One driver who goes round tracks for a living.
explanation.definitionFit: Lance is the first name of the Canadian racing driver Stroll, who competes in Formula One races on circuits worldwide.

clue.text: Gripped by Study in Scarlet you completely changed

indicators.note: whatever is gripped is held in the middle of the hand, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: a den is a private study room
at and in both mean located somewhere
scarlet is a bright red
text-speak spelling

explanation.surface: Reading the Sherlock Holmes story A Study in Scarlet has transformed you entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics push you to read the Conan Doyle title as one unit, but each word is a separate piece, with U held inside the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Denatured means having had its natural qualities altered, as with denatured alcohol or a denatured protein, a thorough change.

clue.text: See bachelor leaving like a shot — awkward!

parts.note: the spoken name of the letter

indicators.note: whoever is leaving goes away, so that letter is removed

parts.note: a backhand is a tennis shot, so backhanded is in the manner of one
B is the abbreviation for bachelor

explanation.surface: An awkward moment: an unmarried man bolts from the room like a shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like a shot' means instantly in the surface, but here it describes a stroke in tennis. Drop the B and put C, the letter that says 'see', in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Cack-handed is British informal slang for clumsy or inept with one's hands, the same as awkward in manner.

clue.text: I almost forgot the way over here

parts.note: a postscript adds something the writer nearly left out
ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: Someone nearly forgot the directions and now points them out here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I almost forgot' reads as a speaker's aside, but it stands for the postscript added to a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Psst is a whispered sound used to catch someone's attention discreetly, just like calling 'over here'.

clue.text: Not sure about one getting time off for lecture

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is placed round another

parts.note: er is the hesitant sound of someone unsure
a means one

indicators.note: something taken off is removed, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: to twig is to get, in the sense of understand
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone uncertain about a person being given time off for a lecture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting' means grasping, twigging in British slang; take the T for time off it and put it after E(A)R.
explanation.definitionFit: An earwigging is British informal slang for a scolding or telling-off, a stern lecture delivered to someone.

clue.text: 'Right, arrest Kemi!' Unlikely he'd say that

definitions.text: 'Right, arrest Kemi!' Unlikely he'd say that

indicators.note: an unlikely arrangement is not the natural one, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
taken as written

explanation.surface: An order to arrest the Conservative leader, which the Labour prime minister would never give.
explanation.walkthrough: Kemi Badenoch leads the Conservatives, Britain's main opposition party; the Labour prime minister would hardly order her arrest. His name is spelt by the clue's own letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the Labour prime minister, a politician who would not order his rival detained.

clue.text: The same boring routine after excitement decreased?

indicators.note: a drill boring into something goes inside it, so one piece enters another
after excitement things are stirred up and thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written
do is short for ditto, the same again

explanation.surface: The same dull daily round has dulled things after all the excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decreased' reads as 'reduced', but split it as de-creased, with creases removed; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes that have had their creases removed with a hot iron have been literally de-creased, the pun the setter intends.

clue.text: During day off sail to island country

indicators.note: what happens during a period falls inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for day
off and out both mean away or not on
a jib is a triangular sail
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: On a day's holiday, someone sails across to an island nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Day off' looks like a holiday, but the words give D and OUT separately, with the sail placed between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Djibouti is a small nation in the Horn of Africa, on the Gulf of Aden.

clue.text: Police breaking in half turned and collapsed

indicators.note: a burglar breaking in ends up inside, so one piece enters another
something turned faces the opposite way, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: demi is a prefix meaning half
the plod is British slang for the police, after Mr Plod in the Noddy books

explanation.surface: Officers burst in halfway, then turned round and fell down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking in' looks like a raid by officers, and 'in half' looks like a phrase, but 'in' belongs to the container signal and 'half' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To implode is to cave or fall inwards, so something that imploded has collapsed in on itself.

clue.text: Carrot or stick in prospect?

parts.note: to jam is to stick fast
something in prospect lies ahead, in the future

explanation.surface: It asks whether a reward or a punishment lies ahead, the classic carrot or stick choice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carrot or stick' reads as one idiom, but 'or' splits it: carrot is the definition, stick starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Jam tomorrow, from Through the Looking-Glass, is a promised reward that never arrives, an incentive like a carrot dangled ahead.

clue.text: Young ladies, half rampant? It made one question one's judgment!

indicators.note: rampant means running wild, and letters running wild end up in a fresh order

parts.note: gals is an informal word for young women
taken as written

explanation.surface: Some girls get a bit wild, and one of them is left doubting her own judgment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' looks like the start of the definition sentence, but it is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To gaslight is to manipulate someone psychologically until they doubt their own perception and sanity, after the film Gaslight.

clue.text: One might cut fish up? Not quite right

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: the ide is a freshwater fish

indicators.note: not quite whole means a little short, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: the Tories are the British party of the political right

explanation.surface: Someone might chop up a fish, though that is not quite the right way to do it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' suggests a knife and a fish, but it is cutting text. 'Right' is the political right, not correct.
explanation.definitionFit: Editors trim and shorten articles, books and films, so they are people whose job is making cuts.

clue.text: See 24 Down
Patriots here from different country

parts.note: something new is different from before
England is a country

explanation.surface: Patriotic people living here came from another country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patriots' looks like flag-wavers, but it is the American football team named after the region.
explanation.definitionFit: The New England Patriots are an NFL franchise based near Boston, so that northeastern region is where the Patriots play.

clue.text: Old boyfriend gets group coming round (it's big up!)

parts.note: an ex is a former partner

indicators.note: coming round means turning to face back, so the letters run in the opposite direction

parts.note: a lot is a group or set of things

explanation.surface: A former boyfriend arrives with a crowd of friends, and makes a big deal of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big up' is British slang meaning to praise or hype someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol is to praise enthusiastically, which is exactly what bigging someone up means in modern slang.

clue.text: Indictment may follow Spooner's order when to stop making beer

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so initial sounds trade places

parts.words: order when to stop making beer
parts.note: an instruction to keep brewing until a set time

explanation.surface: A rule about when brewing must stop could lead to criminal charges.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of 'brew till' and you hear the legal phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A true bill is a grand jury's endorsement that the evidence supports a formal charge, the document on which a prosecution proceeds.

clue.text: On the ground after collapse cycling round junction

indicators.note: after means following, so the later words in the clue are placed next in line rather than ahead
cycling means rotating, so a letter moves from the start of the word to its end

parts.note: to founder is to collapse or sink
O is round in shape
a T-junction is shaped like the letter

explanation.surface: Something lies on the ground after a cyclist collapses going round a junction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' suggests bicycles, but it tells you to move the F of FOUNDER from the front to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Underfoot means beneath one's feet, so whatever is underfoot lies on the ground being walked on.

clue.text: Scots inch closer to success with the French stopping Italy

indicators.note: a stopper sits inside an opening, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: IT is the international code for Italy

indicators.note: the closer of something is what ends it, so only its last letter is taken

parts.note: the closing letter of the word
le is French for the

explanation.surface: The Scots edge closer to winning as the French hold up Italy, a rugby tournament picture.
explanation.walkthrough: Inch is a Scottish word for a small island, as in Inchcolm, not a unit of length.
explanation.definitionFit: An islet is a very small island, which is what the Scottish word inch denotes in place names.

clue.text: Occupied by twisted sequence of hot, lewd nights

indicators.note: something twisted is turned round, so the letters run backwards
a sequence is a run of consecutive letters lifted from the words that follow

parts.note: a run of letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: Someone was taken up with a perverse run of steamy, lewd nights.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the letters backwards from the end of 'hot' into 'nights'.
explanation.definitionFit: To indwell is to live within, an old-fashioned verb, so a place indwelt has been occupied or inhabited.

clue.text: Barge smaller son away

indicators.note: whatever is away is absent, so that letter is removed

parts.note: slighter means smaller or slimmer
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A boat owner sends their younger son off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barge' looks like a verb meaning to push, but it is the flat boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A lighter is a flat-bottomed barge used to carry goods between ships and the quay.
